summary: The chosen world opened in four successive accounts: October 2019 to March 2023 in Swindon and on the downs; Kieran Hale, Barbara Ashby and Laura Russell; the card of twelve words; the wallet first opened on the night bitcoin halved; the 2020 lockdown and yield-farming summer; the grand battle through Kieran's own working day; the house deposit in the stablecoin; the May 2022 collapse; an ending open to the model's draws. The era is real with a documentary cutoff of 31 March 2023. Two claims of the earlier accounts are revised to reconcile with documented prices.

accounts: In October 2019 Kieran Hale, twenty-nine, clears payment exceptions on the third floor of the White Hart Building Society in west Swindon, a job where every week is the same and the systems are older than he is. A flagged forty-thousand-pound transfer brings him Barbara Ashby, sixty-six, who once wrote code for the clearing system he works inside and is moving her savings out of it on purpose. A week later she posts him a card with twelve words and fifty pounds of bitcoin behind them. He should declare the gift and does not. In the spring 2020 lockdown, alone in the flat while his partner Laura Russell works the intensive-care wards, he types the words in, and the small corner of the world he knew opens into a vast playing field: decentralized finance, a chat server called the Sharehouse, yields farmed through the night, and a battle between the old institutions and the new machines that runs straight through his own working day. By the end of 2021 he is rich on paper; in January 2022 their shared house deposit goes into a stablecoin paying nearly twenty percent; in May 2022 the stablecoin breaks. What he does then, and what it costs him, Laura and Barbara, is decided by the model's draws.

Kieran's world is safe and repetitive and older than it looks. His grandfather worked in the railway works until they closed in 1986; his father has built engines at the car plant on the old airfield since 1992 and is waiting for it to close, as announced, in 2021. Kieran joined the Hart at twenty, gave up the online game he had been good at as a teenager, and became the person who knows why a payment failed: every file runs overnight, every exception must be cleared before the cut-off, and a payment takes three working days because it did in 1968. His life is a band of known faces, the tea round, the Thursday quiz, Sunday lunch at his parents', Laura's shift pattern stuck to the fridge. Barbara breaks into it twice: first as a voice on the phone who laughs at his scam-check script and tells him he is standing inside a machine he has never seen, then as a letter addressed to him by name at the exceptions desk. The card is a key he is not allowed to hold. Keeping it is the first secret of his adult life.

The lockdown shrinks his routine to one room and a laptop, and that is where the other world opens: the balance appears when he types the words, the public ledger shows every transaction anyone has ever made, and the summer of 2020 turns money into a game with no closing time. Kieran is good at it. He farms tokens named after food, learns a new language in a week, finds in the Sharehouse the first group since his game that treats him as someone who matters. By day the Hart makes him the expert on its new blocks on payments to crypto exchanges; by night he routes around them. Barbara, whom he finally meets on the downs at Avebury, is a bitcoin purist who calls all of this the old casino in a new costume. Laura, exhausted by two waves of the pandemic, wants a house. In 2021 his father's plant closes, Kieran pays his parents' rent for three months from his gains, and in January 2022 the deposit goes into the stablecoin. In May 2022 it breaks in four days. The old mind that kept him loyal to every band he belonged to keeps him in the game after he understands exactly how it is failing.

October 2019 to March 2020. The blue pill is not a lie; it is a routine that works. Kieran Hale is twenty-nine, reliable, liked, no trouble to anyone, on the exceptions desk of the Hart, a mutual founded by railwaymen in 1868 in a pub. His grandfather's works closed before he was born and the town still keeps its hours. On Monday 21 October 2019 a transfer of forty thousand pounds from a long-standing saver to a crypto exchange trips the scam rules and Kieran makes the call he has made a hundred times. Barbara Ashby, sixty-six, a former railway-works electrician who retrained as a programmer and spent twenty-five years writing software for the interbank clearing, answers his questions with her own: does he know how old the thing he works on is, and who can switch it off? On Friday 1 November a letter arrives addressed to Mr K. Hale, Payments Exceptions, Third Floor. Inside is a card of twelve words and a note: there is fifty pounds behind these; it is yours; go and look. Gifts from customers must be declared. He puts the card in his wallet behind his bus pass and tells no one, not even Laura.

March 2020 to December 2021. On 12 March bitcoin halves in a day; on 23 March the country locks down. Laura goes onto the COVID intensive-care unit and sleeps in the day; Kieran works the batch on a laptop in the spare room. One night in April he types the twelve words into a wallet app, touches the glass to confirm, and the balance comes up: 0.0071 bitcoin, twenty-eight pounds, and behind it a public ledger of every transaction since 2009. It is the corner of a map going dark at the edges. The summer of yield farming turns him into a farmer of tokens named after food who wakes at three to harvest; the Sharehouse, a few thousand anonymous members awake in every time zone, becomes his band. By early 2021 his six thousand pounds is thirty-eight thousand. The grand battle is everywhere: the Hart's compliance team and the regulator's warnings, Barbara's purists against the Sharehouse's gamblers, the new exchanges against the old banks, and Kieran on both sides of it, building the Hart's payment block by day and walking around it by night. Barbara becomes his friend on long walks on the Ridgeway; she tells him the stones at Avebury were dragged there by people who wanted to gather, and that the chat server is the same animal with worse food. His father's plant closes in July 2021. By November 2021 Kieran is worth seventy-one thousand pounds on a screen.

January 2022 to March 2023. As the market falls the Sharehouse moves into 'safe yield': a dollar stablecoin whose savings protocol pays nearly twenty percent. In January the house deposit, twenty-four thousand pounds, fifteen of it Laura's, goes in; how Laura came to be part of that, or not, is drawn from the model. From 9 May 2022 the stablecoin loses its peg; the Sharehouse says it has always come back; the founder's account posts that he is deploying more capital; Kieran understands the mechanism perfectly and holds. By 13 May the deposit is worth a few hundred pounds. The same week the Hart's fraud lines fill with customers who have lost their savings, and Kieran takes their calls in the voice he used on Barbara. What follows is open until drawn: whether and when he tells Laura, what she does, what Barbara does with her own guilt at having handed a key to someone without a map, and what Kieran does with the ancient, loyal, curious mind that took him in. The story ends in March 2023 on the downs, with the three clocks still running: the body's, the institution's and the machine's.

October 2019 to March 2020: the blue pill and the white rabbit. The blue pill is not a lie; it is a routine that works. Kieran Hale, twenty-nine, reliable, liked and no trouble to anyone, sits on the exceptions desk of the Hart, a mutual founded by railwaymen in a pub in 1868. The payments file runs overnight, exceptions are cleared before the ten o'clock cut-off, a payment takes three working days because it did in 1968, and the week has the same shape every week: the 8.12 bus, the tea round, the Thursday quiz at the pub, Laura's rota on the fridge, Sunday lunch at his parents' in Penhill where his father talks about the car plant closing in 2021 as if it were weather. On Monday 21 October 2019 a transfer of forty thousand pounds from a saver of thirty years' standing to a crypto exchange trips the scam rules and Kieran makes the call he has made a hundred times. Barbara Ashby, sixty-six, laughs at the script. She was an electrician in the railway works until they closed, then spent twenty-five years at a Reading bureau writing software for the interbank clearing, including, she says, the bit that waits. She asks him whether he knows how old the thing he works on is, and who could switch it off. On Friday 1 November a letter arrives addressed to Mr K. Hale, Payments Exceptions, Third Floor, White Hart House. Inside is a card of twelve words and a note: there is fifty pounds behind these; it is yours; go and look. Gifts from customers must be declared. Declaring it would make her a case and him a colleague who accepted something. He puts the card in his wallet behind his bus pass and tells no one, not even Laura.

March 2020 to December 2020: the fall and the overwhelm. On the evening of 12 March 2020 the news says bitcoin has halved in a day; Kieran remembers the card, types the twelve words into a wallet app at the kitchen table, touches the glass to confirm, and the balance rises out of nothing: 0.0071 bitcoin, twenty-eight pounds, half of what Barbara gave him, and behind it a public ledger of every transaction since 2009, readable by anyone. On 23 March the country locks down. Laura moves onto the COVID intensive-care unit and sleeps in the day; Kieran works the batch on a laptop in the spare room. The corner of the map he has lived in turns out to have edges, and past them is the biggest game he has ever seen. The summer of yield farming arrives in June: tokens named after food, pools, harvests, governance, gas, impermanent loss, a new word every hour, and his reaction is the one everyone has: what on earth is this. He learns it anyway, fast, the way he learned the game at fifteen. He puts in six thousand pounds in July. The Sharehouse, a few thousand anonymous members awake in every time zone, becomes the first band since the game that treats him as someone who matters. In September, when people may meet outdoors in sixes, Barbara takes him walking from her cottage at Avebury Trusloe up onto the Ridgeway. She is a bitcoin purist who calls decentralized finance the old casino in a new costume, and she tells him that the stones behind them were dragged across the downs by people who wanted to gather.

January 2021 to December 2021: the grand battle and the harvest. The third lockdown sends Laura back to the unit in January for the worst weeks of the pandemic; she comes home and sits in the car outside for twenty minutes before coming up. By February Kieran's six thousand pounds is thirty-eight thousand. The battle between the old world and the new runs straight through his day: the regulator's warnings, the Hart's decision in the summer to block payments to several crypto exchanges, and Kieran, the man who knows why a payment fails, seconded to build the block by day while he walks around it at night through an app the Hart has never heard of. The Sharehouse has its own wars: purists against gamblers, one chain against another, the founders of new protocols against everyone who says they are frauds. His status rises in the band; he answers newcomers at three in the morning; he checks the farm the way his ancestors checked the fields. In July his father's plant closes and Kieran pays his parents' rent for three months from his gains, the best thing the money ever does. By November 2021 he is worth seventy-one thousand pounds on a screen, Laura has started looking at houses in Wroughton, and three clocks are running in him at once: a body built for a band on the downs, an employer built for the three-day batch, and a phone that never closes.

January 2022 to March 2023: the break and the reckoning. As prices fall, the Sharehouse moves into what it calls safe yield: a dollar stablecoin whose savings protocol pays about twenty percent. In January 2022 the house deposit, twenty-four thousand pounds, fifteen of it Laura's overtime, goes in; how Laura came to be part of that, or not, is drawn from the model. From 9 May 2022 the stablecoin slips from its dollar; the Sharehouse says it has always come back; the founder's account posts that he is deploying more capital; Kieran understands the mechanism perfectly and holds, because the band holds and because selling would make it real. By 13 May the deposit is worth about three thousand pounds and falling; by June it is worth a few hundred. The same week the Hart's fraud lines fill with customers who have lost their savings, and Kieran takes their calls in the voice he used on Barbara. What follows is open until drawn: whether and when he tells Laura, what she does, what Barbara does with the guilt of having handed a key to someone without a map, and what Kieran does with the loyal, curious, ancient mind that took him in. In November 2022 a large exchange collapses in the background and Barbara's own coins fall to a quarter of their peak; she says she has seen three of these. The story ends in March 2023 on the downs, with the three clocks still running.
closedQuestions: Kieran Hale: born April 1990 in Swindon; payments exceptions analyst at the White Hart Building Society since 2010; rents a flat in Old Swindon with Laura since 2016.
Laura Russell: born 1991; intensive-care staff nurse at the Swindon hospital since 2017; with Kieran since 2014.

Barbara Ashby: born 1953 in Swindon; electrical apprentice then fitter at the railway works 1969-1986; programmer at a Reading software bureau on interbank clearing software 1988-2013; retired; lives alone in a cottage at Avebury Trusloe; has held bitcoin since 2013.
The White Hart Building Society (the Hart): invented mutual founded in 1868 by railwaymen meeting at a White Hart inn; head office and payments operations in west Swindon; about 1,100 staff.
The Sharehouse: invented chat server of a few thousand anonymous yield farmers.
The flagged transfer: 40,000 pounds from Barbara's Hart savings to a crypto exchange on Monday 21 October 2019; Kieran's scam-check call the same afternoon.
The card: posted by Barbara, arrives Friday 1 November 2019; twelve words; 0.0071 bitcoin, about 50 pounds that day.
Kieran first opens the wallet on the evening of 12 March 2020, the day bitcoin halves, when it is worth about 28 pounds.
Kieran's own stake: 6,000 pounds in July 2020; about 38,000 pounds by February 2021; peak paper value about 71,000 pounds in November 2021.
The house deposit: 24,000 pounds (15,000 Laura's, 9,000 Kieran's) moved into the stablecoin in January 2022; how Laura was involved is drawn.
The collapse: the stablecoin loses its peg from 9 May 2022; by 13 May the deposit is worth about 3,000 pounds and falling; by June a few hundred.
Kieran's father loses his job when the car plant closes in July 2021.
The narrated interval runs from October 2019 to March 2023.
Barbara and Kieran first meet in person in September 2020, walking from Avebury Trusloe onto the Ridgeway.
The Hart decides in summer 2021 to block payments to several crypto exchanges; Kieran is seconded to build the block.
Laura works the COVID intensive-care unit in both the spring 2020 and January 2021 waves.

revisions.claim: Kieran first types the twelve words in one night in April 2020, when the wallet is worth twenty-eight pounds.
revisions.revisedTo: He types them in on the evening of 12 March 2020, the day bitcoin halves, when it is worth about twenty-eight pounds.
revisions.reason: At April 2020 prices 0.0071 bitcoin was worth about forty pounds, not twenty-eight; the twenty-eight-pound value belongs to the crash of 12 March. Moving the moment to that evening also gives it a cause: the news of the crash reminds him of the card.

revisions.claim: By 13 May 2022 the deposit is worth a few hundred pounds.
revisions.revisedTo: By 13 May it is worth about three thousand pounds and falling; by June a few hundred.
revisions.reason: The stablecoin traded around ten to twenty cents on 13 May 2022 and only fell to one or two cents in the following weeks; the numbers must reconcile with the documented path.

era.knowledgeLimit: The recorder's training knowledge covers the whole era and extends beyond it, so no events after the story's end are needed. No research tools were used; each real fact the story uses is recorded as a report citing the public source that documents it, marked as recalled from training knowledge and not consulted in this session.
era.livingPeople: Real organizations and people the story would otherwise touch: the Swindon building societies and banks, the interbank clearing company, the car maker whose Swindon plant closed in July 2021, the algorithmic stablecoin, its savings protocol and its founder, the crypto lenders and exchange that failed later in 2022, the Swindon hospital trust, the regulator. Invented replacements in the foreground: the White Hart Building Society, the Sharehouse, the Reading software bureau Barbara worked for, the stablecoin referred to only as 'the stablecoin' with its savings protocol and a founder's online persona (invented, unnamed or given an invented handle); the car plant, hospital and regulator stay unnamed. Real events stay in the background with their real dates and prices; no living person appears.
